cards.title: Polynomial-pass streaming Vertex Cover
cards.formal: Is there a single streaming algorithm and absolute constants C,D,c>0 such that, for every n≥2, every integer budget 1≤k≤n and every insertion-only edge stream of a simple undirected graph G on vertex set [n], the algorithm uses at most Ck log₂(2n) bits of working memory and at most D(k+1)^c passes, and outputs either a vertex cover of size at most k or NO if no such cover exists? Randomization is allowed, with probability at least 2/3 of a correct output for every fixed input stream. The memory and pass bounds must hold for every input and every outcome of the random bits. Each pass reads the same stream in the same fixed but arbitrary order; the polynomial exponent and constants are independent of n and k.
cards.why: Asks whether repeated access can replace the extra factor of k in the memory needed for exact parameterized graph computation, while retaining only polynomially many scans. This is a basic space-versus-access tradeoff for an NP-hard graph problem.
cards.status_note: Read the full source’s algorithm and question, and the 2024 journal introduction, stream-model definitions, Theorem 45 and auxiliary bipartite-cover lemma. The 2024 paper explicitly retains the solving problem. Searches through 12 September 2026 also found a 2025 Utrecht thesis reiterating the question, but that thesis was checked only through its indexed concluding passage and publication record. No general solution was found; searches are not exhaustive.

progress.text: The source establishes the deterministic 2^k-pass, O(k log n)-bit algorithm and asks for polynomially many passes at the same memory scale.
A 2k-vertex kernel can be emitted as a stream using polynomially many passes and O(k log n) bits; the paper expressly distinguishes this from solving Vertex Cover within those resources.

sentences: The graph arrives as an arbitrary fixed-order stream of edges, and k is a proposed upper bound on a vertex cover’s size.
The target is an exact cover or a correct NO answer using O(k log n) bits and polynomially many passes.
Known algorithms attain that memory bound with 2^k passes, while one-pass solutions use more memory.
Randomized algorithms with constant success probability are allowed, but space and pass bounds are worst case.
A 2024 polynomial-pass kernelization uses the desired memory to emit a small graph; it does not solve that graph within the same resources.

cards.definitions: The input supplies n and k in binary and then the edges {u,v}, 1≤u<v≤n, each exactly once, in an arbitrary order. There are no edge deletions, random-order promise or adjacency queries. Vertex labels use ⌈log₂(n+1)⌉ bits; isolated vertices are included in [n] even if they never occur in the stream. A vertex cover is a subset X⊆[n] such that every edge has at least one endpoint in X. The algorithm must output some such X with |X|≤k when one exists and NO otherwise; neither a minimum-cardinality cover nor a 2-approximation is the target. The value k is a supplied upper budget, not a promise that G has a small cover. A pass is one left-to-right scan of the read-only edge sequence. The stream may be restarted at its beginning between passes but may not be rewritten, reordered, or accessed at arbitrary positions. A partial last scan counts as a pass. The algorithm retains only its bounded working memory across passes. Memory includes stored vertex names, counters, intermediate structures, retained random bits, and any proposed cover that is subsequently read; an output device is write only and cannot serve as additional scratch memory. Randomness consists of fresh independent fair bits; correctness probability is over these bits for each fixed stream, whose order is independent of them. Two-sided error is allowed, meaning that either a false NO or an invalid cover is a failure. The uniform algorithm must halt on every input and every random-bit outcome; total computation time and time per edge have no additional bound, but all workspace is charged. Neither nonuniform advice depending on n,k nor free unbounded-precision storage is allowed. Deterministic algorithms are included as a special case. A constant success probability strictly above 1/2 can be amplified without changing the requested asymptotic memory and pass forms; 2/3 fixes the convention. This card allows bounded-error randomization, consistent with the lower-bound scope of the full source; the existing upper bound it seeks to improve happens to be deterministic. The k=0 case is omitted only because a single scan determines whether the graph is edgeless. There is no restriction k=O(log n). Polynomially many passes means a fixed power of k, independent of n, not a polynomial in n or an arbitrary function of k.
cards.answer_criterion: Give an algorithm with the stated uniform correctness, memory and worst-case pass guarantees, or prove that no bounded-error algorithm can meet them for all n,k and all edge orders. A negative result restricted to deterministic algorithms does not refute the randomized formulation. An algorithm using O(k² log n) space, exponentially many passes, a stronger stream model, or a pre-supplied cover does not meet the target. Producing a small kernel as a separate output stream is insufficient unless the full task is also solved within the same bounds.

context_blocks.title: Known upper bounds trade space for passes
context_blocks.text: The source gives a deterministic exact algorithm using 2^k passes and O(k log n) bits. One-pass algorithms instead use roughly quadratic dependence on k in their memory. The open question asks whether the linear dependence in memory can coexist with only polynomial dependence in the number of passes.

context_blocks.title: Unrestricted computation does not remove the storage restriction
context_blocks.text: The streaming model constrains retained information and access to input rather than computation time. A full graph or a large reduced instance cannot be placed in uncharged memory while an offline solver runs.

context_blocks.title: A later kernel can be emitted using the desired memory
context_blocks.text: The 2024 paper outputs a reduced Vertex Cover instance on at most 2k vertices using O(k³) passes in the edge-arrival model and O(k log n) bits of memory. The reduced graph may still have O(k²) edges. Its introduction explicitly says the polynomial-pass, O(k log n)-space solving question remains open.

context_blocks.title: A bipartite subroutine is not a solver for all graphs
context_blocks.text: The later paper’s small-space minimum-cover lemma concerns an auxiliary bipartite graph and is used in obtaining the reduced instance. It does not compute an exact minimum cover of the original arbitrary graph with the requested resources.

cards.context:
The source gives a deterministic exact algorithm using 2^k passes and O(k log n) bits. One-pass algorithms instead use roughly quadratic dependence on k in their memory. The open question asks whether the linear dependence in memory can coexist with only polynomial dependence in the number of passes.

The streaming model constrains retained information and access to input rather than computation time. A full graph or a large reduced instance cannot be placed in uncharged memory while an offline solver runs.

The 2024 paper outputs a reduced Vertex Cover instance on at most 2k vertices using O(k³) passes in the edge-arrival model and O(k log n) bits of memory. The reduced graph may still have O(k²) edges. Its introduction explicitly says the polynomial-pass, O(k log n)-space solving question remains open.

The later paper’s small-space minimum-cover lemma concerns an auxiliary bipartite graph and is used in obtaining the reduced instance. It does not compute an exact minimum cover of the original arbitrary graph with the requested resources.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
